title: Elodie and the Winter
premise: Sebastian Vane, a meticulous property surveyor, arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for a bank sale and finds a family—widowed mother Ivy and her two children—who insist the house is watching them. The mirrors begin lagging one second behind reality, then showing rooms that don't exist, and Sebastian realizes the house is counting down to the refilling of an old well where, decades ago, the town drowned a woman named Elodie rather than let her testify against them. As the count nears zero, the house begins claiming memories as payment, erasing the family's pasts one by one. In the climax, Sebastian chooses to give up her own documented life—the surveyor's prayer of records—to stand in for Elodie at the well, letting the family escape ahead of the final count; the epilogue shows the house empty, its mirrors running exactly on time, while somewhere a new appraisal file opens itself.
about_author: N. M. Thackeray is the pen name of a former land registry clerk from coastal Maine who spent eleven years cataloguing deeds for houses no one would buy. Their fiction explores what buildings remember when people refuse to.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. She arrives at Hollowmere House with her clipboard, laser measure, and ritual of documentation, meeting reluctant seller Ivy Marsh and her children, Wren and Toby. The house measures wrong: every room comes out slightly larger inside than out. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack into unease.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. While photographing the upstairs hall, she notices her own reflection in a mirror lags—a blink arriving after her eyelid falls. She tests it scientifically and it passes every test except the one that matters. Emotional beat: the rational mind building its first denial.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: POV Wren, age twelve. Wren has been counting the house's sounds—the well pump that cycles even though the well was capped in 1974. She warns Sebastian not to write anything down after dark. Emotional beat: found-family tenderness forming between the outsider and the frightened child.

chapters.title: The Deed and the Drowned
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. At the county archive she pulls the house's history: in 1953, a woman named Elodie Crane accused three prominent men; before she could testify, she was found in the well, ruled a suicide. The deed transfers the same week. Emotional beat: cold archival horror becoming personal mission.

chapters.title: Rooms That Aren't
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. The mirror lag widens to two seconds, and reflections now show a furnished parlor that doesn't exist—Elodie's parlor, preserved behind glass. Ivy admits the family has seen it too and can't afford to leave. Emotional beat: complicity; Sebastian stays when she should go.

chapters.title: Toby's Missing Year
chapters.summary: POV Ivy. Her son Toby forgets his ninth birthday entirely; photographs of it have gone blank. The house is taking payment in memory, oldest and happiest first. Emotional beat: a mother's terror reframed as arithmetic—what will it take next?

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. She discovers tally marks scratched inside every closet door, thousands deep, always in groups that end just short of a number she can't read. The mirror lag now shows the reflection moving independently. Emotional beat: dread shifting from atmosphere to mechanism.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Look Away
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. She canvasses the village; the descendants of the three accused men are polite, generous, and unanimous: sell the house, leave, don't dig. One old man whispers that the well 'refills every fifty years.' Emotional beat: justice outside the law—she realizes the law was the crime.

chapters.title: Wren's Map
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren gives Sebastian her hand-drawn map of the house's sounds and cold spots, which trace a second floor plan beneath the real one—the house as Elodie experienced it. Emotional beat: the child becomes the guide; trust cemented.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Writing everything down seems to slow the memory-loss, so she turns the kitchen into an archive, narrating the family's lives aloud as she records them. For one night, the house is quiet. Emotional beat: fragile hope built on ritual.

chapters.title: The Reflection Speaks
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. In the hall mirror, the lagged image mouths words she finally reads: NOT SUICIDE. WITNESS. The reflection is Elodie—or what the house kept of her—still trying to testify seventy years on. Emotional beat: grief and fury fused.

chapters.title: Ivy Signs
chapters.summary: POV Ivy. Under pressure from the bank and the neighbors, Ivy signs the sale papers; the moment ink dries, the mirror lag snaps to five seconds and Toby loses his name for an hour. Emotional beat: betrayal of self—she sold the house to save the children and endangered them.

chapters.title: The Well Room
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Following Wren's map through a wall that shouldn't open, they find the capped well beneath the kitchen, warm air rising, the cap sweating like skin. The tally marks all converge here. Emotional beat: awe curdling into certainty—they've found the house's heart.

chapters.title: Fifty Years, Fifty Nights
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Cross-referencing dates, she calculates the cycle: the house claims a witness every fifty years, and this year is the fiftieth. The count isn't random—it's a trial that never concluded, reconvening annually until someone testifies. Emotional beat: the horror revealed as unfinished justice.

chapters.title: They Come at Night
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The descendants arrive with movers and lawyers to empty the house before the anniversary night, stripping it of evidence—and the mirrors begin reflecting their faces instead of their bodies. Emotional beat: righteous anger; the children hide Sebastian's archive in the well room.

chapters.title: Payment Refused
chapters.summary: POV Ivy. The house takes Ivy's memory of her late husband whole, leaving her holding a wedding ring she can't explain. She understands at last: it doesn't want payment, it wants a witness, and it will hollow everyone until one steps forward. Emotional beat: sacrificial clarity.

chapters.title: The Trial Reconvenes
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. On the anniversary night the mirrors stop lagging and start showing 1953—the parlor, the three men, Elodie at the door. The house demands the testimony that was stolen. Sebastian reads her entire archive aloud as evidence. Emotional beat: courage as clerical work; the surveyor becomes the court.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Zero
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. The men in the mirror turn toward her; the well uncaps itself below. The house offers a trade—one witness stays, the family walks free with every memory restored. Sebastian sends Ivy, Wren, and Toby out ahead of the final count and takes Elodie's hand. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into choice.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: POV Elodie (first time). Inside the well's dark, the two witnesses finish what 1953 interrupted: names spoken, crimes named, the record sealed. The house exhales. Emotional beat: catharsis—justice rendered outside any law that ever failed her.

chapters.title: On Time
chapters.summary: POV Wren. From the car, Wren watches every window of Hollowmere go dark at once, then sees her brother remember his birthday, her mother remember her husband. The mirrors, visible through the door left open, reflect the empty hall exactly on time. Emotional beat: release and survivor's guilt intertwined.

chapters.title: The New File
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian (ambiguous). She wakes in a sunlit version of Elodie's parlor with her clipboard, unhurried, unafraid, cataloguing a house that finally holds still. Whether she is dead, kept, or at peace is left to the reader. Emotional beat: strange serenity.

chapters.title: Appraised Value
chapters.summary: POV omniscient/epistolary. A bank clerk months later finds the completed Hollowmere appraisal in the system: condition excellent, occupancy one, recommended action—leave standing. The last line of the report reads, in Sebastian's handwriting, 'Documented. Witnessed. Paid in full.' Emotional beat: quiet closure with one cold shiver.
